geneesmiddelenwet.definition: The Dutch Medicines Act. It says what a medicine is, who may make, sell and advertise one, and what happens if someone breaks the rules.

medicine-by-presentation.definition: A product counts as a medicine if it is presented as treating or preventing disease. Words, pictures, claims and the shape of the product all count, not only the label.

medicine-by-function.definition: A product counts as a medicine if it can really change how the body works through a drug-like effect. Courts look at what the substance does, case by case.

cjeu.term: Court of Justice of the European Union
cjeu.definition: The highest court for EU law, in Luxembourg. When a national court asks it what an EU rule means, its answer binds courts in every EU country.

eu-directive.definition: A type of EU law that tells every EU country what result to reach. Each country then writes the rules into its own national law.

eu-regulation.definition: A type of EU law that applies directly in every EU country, without a national law in between.

centralised-procedure.definition: The EU route to approve a medicine for all EU countries at once. The EMA assesses it and the European Commission decides.

marketing-authorisation-holder.definition: The company that holds the licence for a medicine. It is responsible for the medicine's quality and must collect and report its side effects.

gmp.definition: The quality rules for making medicines. They cover clean rooms, trained staff, tested ingredients, checks on every batch and records that inspectors can see.

pharmacopoeia.definition: An official book of quality standards for medicines and their ingredients. It says how pure a substance must be and how to test it.

magistral-preparation.definition: A medicine that a pharmacy makes itself for one named patient, on a doctor's prescription. It needs no marketing authorisation, but it must still meet quality rules.

administrative-fine.definition: A fine that a government body such as the IGJ gives itself, without going to a criminal court.

economic-offences-act.definition: A Dutch law that makes breaches of certain other laws, such as parts of the Medicines Act, into criminal offences. Done on purpose, they count as crimes.

aliases: Netherlands Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority
nvwa.definition: The Dutch food and consumer product safety authority. Together with the IGJ it watches over the Medicines Act.

eu-common-logo.definition: The logo that legal online sellers of medicines in the EU must show. Clicking it should lead to a government list where the seller is registered.

safety-features.definition: A unique code and a seal on the box of most prescription medicines in the EU. Pharmacies scan the code to check that the pack is genuine.

clinical-trials-regulation.definition: The EU law on testing medicines in people. It sets rules for approval, consent and openness, and has applied since 31 January 2022.

ctis.definition: The EU's online system for clinical trials. Companies apply through it, and the public part lets anyone search for trials in the EU.

aliases: Central Committee on Research Involving Human Subjects
ccmo.definition: The Dutch central committee for research in people. It supervises the ethics committees and reviews some studies itself.

metc.definition: A committee of doctors, lawyers and others that checks a study plan before it may start. It asks whether the study is useful and not too risky for the people in it.

aliases: Federal Agency for Medicines and Health Products
famhp.definition: Belgium's medicines agency. It approves and checks medicines, collects side-effect reports and acts against illegal medicines.

medical-need-programme.definition: In Belgium, a programme that lets doctors use an approved medicine for a serious illness it is not yet approved for, while that use is being studied or assessed.

out-of-court-settlement.definition: A sum you can pay to close a case, so that it does not go to a criminal court.

nado.definition: The body that runs doping tests and anti-doping rules in a country or region. Belgium has four.

intended-use.definition: In US law, what a seller really means a product to be used for. The FDA judges it from all the seller's words and actions, not only from the label.

investigators-brochure.definition: Files a company writes about an experimental medicine for a trial. The Investigator's Brochure is for the trial doctors. The IMPD is for the regulator. Together they describe how it is made and what animal and human studies found.

eea.definition: The European Economic Area: the EU countries plus Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein. They share the EU rules on medicines.

smpc.definition: The official description of a licensed medicine for doctors and pharmacists. It lists what the medicine is for, the approved doses, side effects, warnings and interactions.

mra-country.definition: A country outside the EU that has an agreement with the EU to accept each other's checks on how medicines are made.

big-register.definition: The Dutch public register of licensed health professionals, such as doctors and pharmacists. Only a doctor in this register may sign a doctor's declaration.
